newsitem.title: THAILAND: Burma vows to clear Karen rebels from border.
newsitem.headline: Burma vows to clear Karen rebels from border.

text.p: Burma's military government vowed on Monday to clear out rebel Karen National Union (KNU) guerrillas from its eastern border because they posed a threat to the country's political, economic and social security.

The KNU was responsible for sabotage in Burmese urban and rural areas and had encouraged anti-government guerrilla movements that had returned to the legal fold to return to insurgency, a government statement received by Reuters said.
"If they are allowed to continue in that manner, it (the KNU) will become not only a threat to national security but will harm the nation politically, economically and socially as well," it said.

Burmese troops drove KNU mobile camps from the country's eastern border area adjoining Thailand last week, sparking an exodus of thousands of Karen refugees into Thailand, Thai border police and refugee sources said.
Thai military sources from near the western Thai border town of Mae Sot said there were no new reports of fighting between the KNU and Burmese troops.

The Burmese statement denied those fleeing were refugees. "We have again and again said in the past that if not all, the high majority of those people staying in these camps are family members of the KNU," it added.
"The government has been and is always willing to have a meaningful peace negotiation with the KNU. The door to the peace talks is always open," it added.
Hardline KNU leader Bo Mya told a Thai newspaper on Monday that he would continue to fight Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) despite the setbacks.
Some KNU sources said a split appeared to be developing within the KNU as some leaders said that Bo Mya, with his hardline stance, was an obstacle to the progress of the KNU.

Bo Mya has rejected several peace overtures from Rangoon and insisted that the KNU, founded in 1948 to seek greater autonomy for the Karen state, would not lay down arms as a precondition to peace talks.

Rebel sources told Reuters on Monday the umbrella National Democratic Front (NDF) of 10 rebel organisations chose KNU vice-president General Swe Seing to replace Bo Mya as its new leader after a weeklong meeting ending on Sunday.
Swe Seing, 70, is seen as the most powerful figure in the KNU and is tipped by some in the KNU to eventually replace Bo Mya in that organisation as well.

During the meeting in eastern Kayah state, the NDF agreed to cooperate militarily against the SLORC but was unable to reach a common view on a KNU proposal that now may be the time to hold peace talks with Rangoon, sources said.

"We have reached a solution on the appointment of General Swe Seing as the chairman of NDF to replace the old man (Bo Mya) and also agreed on military cooperation in fighting against the SLORC," Khun Kyaw Oo, a senior delegate from the Shan United Revolution Army (SURA) said by telephone.
Among the 10 organisations in the NDF are the KNU, the SURA and groups representing the Wa, the Chin, the Mon, the Kokang and the Karenni Progress Party (KNPP).

The alliance formed in the 1970s was a thorn in the Burmese government's flesh in the 1980s but its influence declined from the early 1990s when splinter groups emerged and some of its members reached ceasefire agreements with the Burmese government.
The SLORC maintains that at least 15 rebel faction have made ceasefire accords with the government.
